tells: A specific and memorable idea that only this piece could have: the world is a clockwork map whose cities unfold from gears, with an astrolabe sun at the centre. The concept also works as a recap device and as an orientation tool for the viewer
Dense, layered frames: engraved bands carrying narrative reliefs, mechanical towers, a parchment map with rivers, sun rings, and an emblem lockup. Every frame works as a poster
Typography has a point of view. Credits are set in a carved display face with small house sigils beside the names, and the logotype is integrated into the ironwork emblem
Warm sepia and brass with burnt-out sunlight, and real tooling and wood-and-metal textures throughout
Clear choreography: the frames move from the band, to cities unfolding, to the gear spire, to the astrolabe, to the map, to the emblem, as one continuous flight through a single machine
gaps: The flare and blooming on the brass are pushed hard in places and flatten detail at the extremes
Credit placement occasionally fights busy mechanical detail, for example over the spire and the map, and legibility suffers
The palette is strong but conventional for fantasy. A less expected colour hold would raise it further

tells: Type-led kinetic piece with a strong system: modular Latin letters are cut into fragments and mixed with katakana-like glyphs, so the Latin/Japanese pun is built into the letterforms

Each frame uses a different layout: a giant cropped 'D' with a target ring, a horizontal letter band, a framed grid of scattered glyphs, a diagonal slash with confetti-like strokes, a pixel-dot matrix of letters, and a collage lockup
Deliberate, unusual palette: hot pink, mint cyan, acid lime and violet on a near-black ground. The colour holds change from frame to frame but stay within one system
Texture is designed in through halftone dots, scanline grain, pixel matrices and print misregistration
The frames imply varied choreography, with scrolling, scattering, rotation and dot-matrix rebuilding, and the end lockup pulls the motifs together
gaps: The idea is mostly a formal type system. B has a narrative or world concept that makes it memorable beyond the style
The glitch and pixel vocabulary of the late 2010s risks reading as a genre exercise. One move that belongs only to this subject would set it apart
The frames are flat: they have depth of layering but no light. A dimensional or physical element would add the material richness that B and A carry

tells: The macro photography of molten, cooling metal forming into jewelled regalia makes 'the crown being made' the idea itself, and it belongs to this subject only
The light is real and motivated: a low-key raking light picks out specular glints on gold and the facets of the gemstones, with smoke and haze adding depth
The credits are set in a carefully chosen spaced Trajan-like roman with small-cap role labels, placed asymmetrically to sit against the image, never on top of it
The sequence builds from raw ore to finished gem to the title card, and each frame changes scale and angle (rough mass, filament, fully worked setting)
The palette is deliberately limited to black, bronze and cold silver, which suits a period drama about royalty
gaps: Every shot uses the same move (shallow-focus macro drifting across metal), so it lacks the structural surprise and change of mode that B gets from moving between map and mechanism
The end title is centred on an almost empty dark ground, a safe and slightly generic resolve compared with the built, lit emblem in B
The dark-luxury macro look is an established genre language; it needs one unexpected cut or a change in scale to push it beyond the category

tells: The concept is specific and memorable: the world as a clockwork map, with cities and castles cranking up out of the terrain, and the device doubles as a guide to the show's geography
The frames are dense and layered, with engraved astrolabe bands showing dragon iconography, miniature cities, gears and sigils, so every frame works as a poster
There is real material texture (worn wood, tarnished brass, engraved leather) and strong motivated light: a central sun flares through the astrolabe and the shadows are tabletop-scale

The frames show varied choreography: a close-up of the band, a low aerial over a city, a tower mechanism rising, a sweep of the armillary rings, a flat map with a pin, and the resolve on the emblem title
The type has a point of view: a custom-flavoured inscriptional serif, with heraldic sigil icons attached to each credit and labels set into the map itself
gaps: The credit placement in the lower third of the mid-sequence frames gets slightly lost against busy detail; the type could integrate more boldly with the mechanisms
The warm sepia grade is used throughout; a deliberate colour shift between regions would add a contrasting chapter
The final logo lockup is heavier and more conventional than the inventive frames that lead up to it

tells: The typography is the subject: Latin glyphs break down into katakana-like fragments, pixel-grid letterforms and segmented display characters, which is a real typographic idea about Tokyo and signage systems
The palette is unusual and deliberate (hot pink, mint cyan, acid lime, violet on a near-black ground) and stays controlled throughout

Every frame has a different structure (large modular letters, horizontal band scan, framed glyph field, diagonal rotated grid, LED dot-matrix, layered collage resolve), which shows choreography and escalation
Printed or riso-like grain and texture on the flat colour fields stop it from looking vector-default
The final frame builds 'TOKYO' as a dense layered collage, a payoff that is earned by the earlier frames
gaps: It sits within a well-known glitch/HUD/kinetic-type genre language; it needs a sharper idea specific to this subject to rival B's concept
There is no real light or depth; everything is flat graphic planes, while B gets its emotion from material and illumination
Readability and hierarchy break down in the busiest frames (the dot-matrix frame especially), so the narrative message is weaker than the visual energy

Physical material is everywhere: engraved metal bands, wood, brass gears, parchment map, with motivated light coming from a central astrolabe sun
